searchText: <@755590043632140352> the other option is to use binary curve over F_2^k , these curves are NOT broken yet but considered potentially the weakest family (with no evidence so far....) That was Kev suggestion above but I couldn't find a Golang implementation of any. Given that the benches I found are much worse than Ristretto I suppose that Ristretto is the way to go for now there are binary curves standardized by nist , i am sure you'll find some implementation Can you point me to one that you guess could be performant as Ristretto? I can try running benches on the MSM It should be relatively simple for me to switch from one curve to another these curves (binary) are usually really fast BUT I thought that for you is really impprtant to have a small p (and binary curve have the smalles p =2) while the binary curves and koblitz binary curve are nist standard (EG K-283) they never gain any popularity because people are "scared" so far noone found an attack on those though found this https://github.com/deatil/go-cryptobin/blob/81cc2c63eda1f694396d945764762926d4cf2f19/elliptic/nist/nist_curves.go#L78 but i would not use in production 😄 If we can get a massive reduction in bandwidth with Ristretto, I would go with that for now, since you can always change it to something more efficient in the future i agree ristretto is a good choice (i personally like more prime order curves though) BUT AFAIU of this protocol it it's optimal to have smaller 'p' ristretto p (hence its coefficients) are 250-ish bits I don't know how much is saved when going from secp256k1 to Ristretto255 -- If it's negligible, then I would also choose secp256k1 since the former is already in the protocol
